content: The Erlang unit, denoted as E, is a dimensionless measure used in telephony to quantify the volume of telecommunications traffic. It is named after the Danish telephone engineer A.K. Erlang, who pioneered traffic engineering and queuing theory. A traffic load of one Erlang corresponds to a single resource being continuously in use, or equivalently, two channels being utilized at 50% capacity each, and so on proportionally. For example, 5 Erlangs of traffic could represent five channels fully in use or ten channels at 50% utilization. Alternatively, an Erlang can be interpreted as a usage multiplier per unit time, where 100% usage equals 1 Erlang, 200% usage equals 2 Erlangs, and so forth. For instance, if the total cell phone usage in a specific area over one hour amounts to 180 minutes, this corresponds to 180/60 = 3 Erlangs. In general, if the mean arrival rate of new calls is denoted as λ (calls per unit time) and the mean call holding time is h, the traffic in Erlangs (A) is given by the product λh. This metric is used to assess whether a system is over-provisioned (too many resources allocated) or under-provisioned (too few resources allocated). For example, traffic measured during peak hours can help determine the number of voice lines required in a T1 or E1 circuit group. If no more than 12 out of 24 channels are expected to be in use at any given time, the remaining 12 channels could be repurposed for data transmission. Traffic measured in Erlangs is also used to calculate the grade of service (GoS) or quality of service (QoS). Various Erlang formulas, such as Erlang B, Erlang C, and the Engset formula, are employed for these calculations. These formulas are derived using a specific type of continuous-time Markov process known as a birth-death process. Erlang B Formula The Erlang B formula assumes an infinite population of sources (e.g., telephone subscribers) collectively offering traffic to N servers (e.g., links in a trunk group). The arrival rate of new calls (birth rate) is constant and denoted as λ, independent of the number of active sources, due to the assumption of an infinite source population. The departure rate of calls (death rate) is proportional to the number of calls in progress, divided by h, the mean call holding time. This formula calculates the blocking probability in a loss system, where a request is aborted if it cannot be served immediately upon arrival. In such systems, requests are not queued. Blocking occurs when a new request arrives, but all servers are already occupied. The formula assumes that blocked traffic is immediately cleared. It can be expressed recursively to facilitate the creation of Erlang B tables: B: The probability of blocking N: The number of resources (e.g., servers or circuits) in a group A: The total offered traffic in Erlangs, calculated as λh The Erlang B formula is applicable to loss systems, such as telephone networks (both fixed and mobile), that do not provide traffic buffering. It assumes that call arrivals follow a Poisson process but is valid for any statistical distribution of call holding times. Erlang B is primarily used as a trunk sizing tool for voice switch-to-voice switch traffic. Erlang C Formula The Erlang C formula also assumes an infinite population of sources offering traffic of A Erlangs to N servers. However, unlike Erlang B, if all servers are busy when a request arrives, the request is queued. An unlimited number of requests can be held in the queue simultaneously. This formula calculates the probability of queuing for offered traffic, assuming that blocked calls remain in the system until they can be served. It is commonly used to determine the number of agents or customer service representatives required to staff a call center, based on a specified desired probability of queuing. A: The total offered traffic in Erlangs N: The number of servers Pw: The probability that a customer must wait for service The Erlang C formula assumes that call arrivals can be modeled by a Poisson process and that call holding times follow a negative exponential distribution. Engset Formula The Engset formula, named after T.O. Engset, is similar to the Erlang formulas but deals with a finite population of S sources rather than the infinite population assumed by Erlang. The formula accounts for the fact that the arrival rate of new calls decreases as more sources (e.g., telephone subscribers) become busy and are therefore unable to originate new calls. When N equals S, the formula simplifies to a binomial distribution. E: The probability of blocking A: The traffic in Erlangs generated by each idle source S: The number of sources N: The number of servers The Engset formula assumes that call arrivals can be modeled by a Poisson process and that call holding times follow a negative exponential distribution. However, due to the finite number of sources, the arrival rate of new calls diminishes as more sources become occupied.
